rows.title: Leadership and Integrity
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Compare and contrast the concepts of leadership, management, integrity, and ethics
Compare and contrast transactional leadership and transformational leadership
Explain the relationship between organizational culture and developing community trust
Describe the process of forming effective teams and developing effective team dynamics
objectives: discuss the ethical, legal, social, and moral complexity of processes within the Administration of Justice system and how they relate to other fields;
explain the impact of effective interpersonal communication within the Administration of Justice system;
recognize the behaviors and decisions that impact personal success and organizational integrity;
describe the potential impact on community trust when personal and organizational integrity is violated;
describe behaviors that improve communication and interactions within the community;
explain five elements of organizational culture that impact the effectiveness of individuals and teams;
describe the difference between management and leadership;
demonstrate the impact of transactional leadership and transformational leadership on individuals and organizations;
identify ethical issues that often arise in regard to professional responsibility, public service, or law;
state basic general ethical principles and to apply these to particular cases;
demonstrate mastery of at least one method for resolving ethical disagreements;
explain the importance - both for one's self and for society as a whole - of being ethical;
propose and defend standards for justice.

rows.title: Investigative Reporting

outcomes: Record information accurately in a police report for the purpose of follow-up investigation and the issuance of complaints.
Use effective written and oral communication to gather information, report and articulate information, analyses, or findings to relevant end users in the legal community.
Synthesize forensic, evidential, and investigatory Information from multiple sources to generate theories about a crime..
objectives: record and use investigation notes;
recite the advantages and disadvantages of form and narrative types of reporting;
describe the physical content of arrest, incident, and other reports and the rationale for different reporting styles;
explain the requirements for effective communication and how to find and assemble information;
record information accurately and legibly enough in a police report to present to others in the legal community for purpose of follow-up investigation and the issuance of complaints;
demonstrate how to provide effective testimony in court as a witness;
demonstrate the ability to write clear, concise and detailed investigative reports with a high level of grammatical accuracy.

define and explain direct and circumstantial evidence;
explain the concept of relevancy with regard to evidence;
explain the rules covering the admissibility of evidence in court;
explain the qualifications related to witness competency;
explain the concept of "chain of custody" and its relationship to the admissibility of evidence;
explain the exclusionary rule as it relates to search and seizure, identification procedures and the admissibility of evidence;
demonstrate an understanding how to testify effectively.

objectives: Define the scope of anthropology and discuss the role of cultural anthropology within the discipline;
Recognize the methods, theories and perspectives used to study and understand human cultures;
Employ the relativist perspective while discussing cultural variation;
Explain the importance of the ethnographic method in the study of culture;
Demonstrate an understanding of anthropological concepts including ethnicity, gender, political organization, economic systems, kinship, rituals and belief systems;
Explain the interconnectedness of the economic, political and sociocultural forces of globalization amongst diverse cultural groups;
Analyze and evaluate the ethical issues anthropologists encounter, and professional ethical obligations that must be met in the study of and application in cultural groups different from their own.

rows.title: Bus Maintenance
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: effectively use rulers, tape measures, vernier calipers, dial calipers, micrometers, dial indicators, brake stack height tools, laser temperature guns, tachometers, multi-meters (basics + VDC), pressure transducers (conversion of psi and in hg.), torque wrenches (conversion of units in. lbs., ft. lbs., nm.) Recognize and use different fastener types, bolts, nuts, washers, and screws; recognize bolt and nut markings and hardness grades class; measure bolts, count threads per inch, measure thread pitch, and use pitch gauges and torque charts. Use basic hand and power tools such as drills, impact guns, and wrenches. Repair threads, use extractors and the correct thread repair inserts, cut and assemble Aeroquip nylon braided hose and fitting.

inspect filters (HVAC, air, coolant, hydraulic fluid, fuel, DEF dosing valve, transmission, and engine oil); remove and install retaining rings, snap rings, e-rings, and circlips; remove and install roll and cotter pins; inspect and replace sealing rings (O-rings, square cut O-rings, and crush washers). Inspect and replace gaskets (paper, cork, metal, silicone, and print-o-seal). Select the correct type and size of hose clamps and apply the correct type and size of hoses and fittings. Use grease, lubricants, cleaners, thread lockers, anti-seize, and RTV silicone. Inspect and test lubricant and hydraulic oils, inspect coolant concentration, measure boiling point, and pressure test the cooling system. Inspect and test diesel and gasoline fuels and diesel exhaust fluid. Check fluids and maintain the Allison b400 and b500, Voith 3e, 5, and 6 transmissions. Perform BMD 14-01 air system tests with instructions and perform the BMD 13-05 cooling system pressure test with instructions.

perform basic inspections of driveline, suspension, and steering components, as well as tire wear and lubricating points. Check brake throws and lubricate the drum brakes. Use Quickserve to maintain Cummings ISL, ISB, ism, and Detroit S60 engines (lubrication, cooling, fueling, air handling intake, and exhaust). Inspect disc brake components. Perform charging system tests, load test batteries 8d and group 31, and perform electrical tests and electrical wiring repairs.
objectives: apply basic principles of measuring, tooling, hardware, materials, and system components toward maintaining heavy-duty diesel engines;
Implement the appropriate standard operating procedures for preventive maintenance Inspections to include California Highway Patrol out-of-service criteria;
identify, inspect, and maintain coach components;
access and use fleet service manuals;
process major inspection forms.

rows.title: Bus Basic Electrical
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: perform basic electrical diagnosis on heavy-duty coach systems. Test batteries, charging system, and cranking system suing specialty equipment. Understand the operation of switches, fusees, relays, motors, solenoids and other electrical devices typically found in a coach bus;

check fuses and/or circuit breakers. Check for power with the ignition key in the different positions; use several electrical testing tools to trace circuit problems due to shorts, opens, high resistance, and lose connections. Use digital multi meters (DMMs) to measure voltage, resistance, and current. Use amp clamps, test lights and digital storage oscilloscopes to help locate problems with sensors and small signal components;

calculate equivalent resistance in series, parallel and series-parallel circuits. Identify standard electrical and electronic components. Understand writing diagrams, wire gauge, wire cool coding and wiring standards. Perform wiring and connector repairs using crimps, solder, and wiring isolation materials. Repin connectors and replace terminals. Build basic series, parallel, and series-parallel circuits and test their operation; identify and use circuit protection devices, understand fuse box design and troubleshoot problems on circuits operated by relays; identify faulty relays;

perform basic electrical tests such as voltage drop, available voltage, continuity and resistance, and current flow tests. Perform basic diagnosis of electrical systems such as blower motor, lighting, charging, cranking, and interior accessories. Perform Midtronics tests and power supply testing; perform power flow tests and work with wiring diagrams to determine a diagnosis strategy.
objectives: understand the fundamental principles and applications of electricity;
apply Ohms, Kirchhoff, and Watts laws;
demonstrate the function and operation of essential electrical components;
demonstrate the proper use and functions of digital multimeters, carbon piles load testers;
perform battery testing using a Midtronics battery impedance tester;
test battery electrolyte strength using a hydrometer;
understand the operation and use of electric and electronic components, and use them to build simple circuits;
understand the use of connectors, switching devices, and electric controls;
understand the basic operation of wiring schematics;
understand the basic operation of electrical systems typical of heavy-duty coach buses;
understand the basic operation of starting system operation and their troubleshooting;
understand the basic operation of charging systems and their troubleshooting;
understand the use and selection of circuit protection devices.

demonstrate correct grammar, sentence structure, and format in the submitted pieces;

rows.title: Studies in Shakespeare
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

outcomes: analyze Shakespeare's works in relation to their historical and cultural context, with attention to identifying unstated premises and hidden assumptions as well as overt themes and messages;
demonstrate knowledge of the structures of the works studied and analyze them in terms of such literary components as plot, character, tone, style and figurative uses of language;
demonstrate understanding of the particular contributions of Shakespeare to literature in English, as well as his works' diverse resonances in contemporary culture.
objectives: recognize differences in approach, style, and technique in Shakespeare's early, middle and late plays;
demonstrate understanding of defining formal and thematic elements of Shakespearean comedies, histories, tragedies and romances and distinguish their differences;
demonstrate understanding of and be able to read and interpret Shakespearean blank verse;
demonstrate understanding of and analyze the plays in performance, with reference to traditional and modern (stage and/or film) adaptations;
analyze Shakespeare's plays in the context of the Elizabethan view of the world;
identify patterns in Shakespeare's work in poetry and drama.

respond to a topic, demonstrate critical thinking, comprehension and use of text to support ideas;
demonstrate sentence-level fluency and control of grammar;

access background knowledge in the subject area;
establish own purpose for reading the material;

take charge of reading, applying strategies to unlock the meaning from texts, including

formulating a controlling idea to focus writing;
supporting each point with adequate and varied evidence; tailoring writing to address a specific audience;
develop sentences to relate and emphasize ideas including detecting and correcting major mechanical and grammatical errors.

pre-read material in order to form questions that promote comprehension, recall and critical thinking;

respond accurately and thoroughly to the assignment; and

fiction;

demonstrate familiarity with major archetypes, themes, and motifs of young adult literature;
apply literary concepts such as narrative structure, characterization, theme, diction, and symbolism to primary texts written for young readers;
critically evaluate and compare works of fiction based on their literary qualities and offer critical responses to the writings of others;

rows.title: Modern and Contemporary U.S. Literature
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with the self-expressed perspectives of the represented groups.
Demonstrate familiarity with the structure and literary devices of the works studied
Read and appreciate the diversity of the literature while identifying some common themes
objectives: demonstrate familiarity with and have developed a critical perspective on the varied achievements in literature by American writers since the mid-19th Century;
analyze literary works in relation to their historical, social and cultural contexts;

demonstrate knowledge of the structure of the works studied and analyze their literary components, including plot, character, tone, style, and figurative uses of language (such as metaphor, irony, symbol, paradox);
contrast the diversity of the works while comparing their treatment of common themes, especially in response to social and political changes;
critically evaluate distinctive eras and chronology of American literature since the mid-19th Century: Realism, Modernism, Harlem Renaissance, Contemporary Literature.

demonstrate knowledge of how cultural/historical lenses have shaped what is or is not considered “literature” or worthy of study, with particular attention to the late 20th century opening of the canon to reflect multi-cultural voices.
demonstrate understanding of how literature both reflects and helps create history and culture;
prepare a research-based project on a genre, a theme, or a school of thought in American literature.

rows.title: The Literature of the Holocaust

The student should be able to evaluate and analyze the role poetry from different times and cultures assumes in coming to terms with the Nazi Holocaust
The student should be able to recognize different generes and styles in Holocaust Literature and their similarities with and differences from other "topical" writing.
objectives: identify the different kinds of Holocaust literature, as well as the similarities and differences between this literature and other “topical” literature;
discuss when these works appeared, how they have evolved, and why they were first—and continue to be—written;
demonstrate familiarity with the structures of the works studied and identify techniques such as irony, analogy, metaphor, allusion, and satire as common to the works read;
recognize the diversity of the literature while identifying common themes (including the problems posed by a fiction which re-imagines an inconceivably harsh reality);
demonstrate understanding of the various ways the literature represents its subject matter depending on the culture and time within which it was produced.
rows.objectives_lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

rows.title: Critical Thinking and Writing through Literature
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: organize a paper so that it is unified and coherent;
respond to a topic, demonstrate critical thinking, comprehension and use of text to support ideas;
demonstrate a sentence-level fluency and control of grammar.
objectives: Critically read, analyze, compare, and evaluate diverse complex literary texts;
Reflect critically on one’s own thought processes to identify and avoid cognitive biases and
common fallacies of language and thought;

Compose thesis-driven arguments to suit a variety of rhetorical situations, including interpretation, evaluation, and literary analysis, supporting them with a variety of appropriate textual evidence and examples;
Identify a text's premise(s) and/or assumptions in various social, historical, cultural, psychological, or aesthetic contexts;

Analyze and employ logical and structural methods such as inductive and deductive reasoning, causation, and supporting claims with reasons, evidence, and responding to diverse perspectives and values;
Find, analyze, interpret, and evaluate primary and secondary sources, incorporating them into written work using appropriate documentation format without plagiarism;

Draft and revise writing for style, diction, and tone showing awareness of audience and social context, and the purpose of the specific writing task; engage in a revision process so that language use does not impede clarity or disrupt meaning;
Identify key elements of major genres (including poetry, drama, fiction) in order to analyze and interpret texts;
Define common literary terms and apply these to analysis of specific texts.
EXPANDED COURSE OBJECTIVES:
Demonstrate critical thinking and reading skills in literary analysis;
Recognize and analyze how racism, xenophobia, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, ableism, and classism shape the contexts for thinking, reading, and writing about literature;
Examine what constitutes “literature” in different eras and societies, considering counter-narratives as well as established “canons”;
Demonstrate active reading and note taking strategies, emphasizing close reading of literary texts;
Appreciate the relationship between language and meaning -- including literal and figurative language, connotation and denotation;
Use logical and structural principles to develop ideas, including inductive and deductive reasoning, cause and effect, and logos, pathos, and ethos;
Demonstrate understanding of formal and informal fallacies in language and thought;

Produce and defend interpretations of literature in major genres based on analysis of themes and literary elements such as characters, setting, point of view, and imagery, and literary modes such as comedy, tragedy, or satire, while also drawing on personal knowledge, experiences and each student’s cultural capital;
Recognize historical structures of privilege and oppression as they are expressed in literary works, as well as the diverse cultural experiences accessible through literature;
Recognize the similarities and differences between the intentions, biases, assumptions, and arguments of an author and his/her/their character(s);
Demonstrate composition skills;
Employ writing process strategies to generate, organize, edit, and present thesis-driven essays with increasing independence;
Compose interpretative and aesthetic responses, making use of summary, paraphrase, and direct quotation;
Select and appropriately integrate quotations and details from primary literary texts and secondary sources as evidence to support a thesis and related claims;
Write with clarity and precision, considering audience and purpose, demonstrating appropriate academic discourse and the conventions of literary analysis;
Demonstrate appropriate research techniques;
Formulate a productive research question;
Demonstrate familiarity with library resources, and identify and evaluate sources appropriate for literary research;
Efficiently gather, record, and organize information;
Integrate source material into the paper, correctly utilizing academic systems of documentation (MLA).

determine if a structural system meets its design specifications, and/or determine how the system will fail, given or having calculated the stresses, strains and displacements.

learn and apply various force system resultants: the moment of a force, cross product, the principle of moments, and the moment of a couple;
construct free-body diagram and analyze the applied equations of equilibrium;

Students will be able to use verbal, written and illustrative means to communicate their understanding of environmental science concepts and laboratory methods.
objectives: apply the principles and philosophies of science;
describe the laws of energy and energy transformations by autotrophy and heterotrophy in food chains;
explain the principles and mechanisms of evolution and relate them to the diversity of life;
analyze interactions and changes that occur among organisms and the environment at the population, community, and ecosystem levels;
describe cultural changes, human population growth, and the impact humans have had on the environment through history.
rows.objectives_lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

rows.title: Introduction to Environmental Studies

Articulate core concepts and methods from the social sciences as they pertain to the design and evaluation of environmental policies and institutions.
Describe the ethical, cross-cultural, and historical contexts of environmental issues and the links between human and natural systems.
Assess how human activities, including the use of energy and natural resources, affect the natural environment, and how those activities have changed since the period of the Industrial Revolution.
objectives: describe Environmental Studies as an interdisciplinary field of study and its position in relationship to the social sciences, humanities, and natural science;
define and apply ecological concepts to modern life in an increasingly technologically conscious society;
assess how the history of human activities and natural resources exploitation has affected Earth's resource inventory and natural processes;
explain the impacts of the Industrial Revolution and subsequent stages of technological advances on environmental change, resources degradation, and the relationship between humans and nature;
compare and contrast the history of land use ethics in Western versus non-Western cultures;
evaluate the influences of the conservation and environmental movements in the United States;

explain how political processes in the United States interact with awareness of environmental change, and how our governmental and legal systems operate to influence public policies and regulations in regard to the environment;

describe the current state of natural resource inventories in the United States, and how effective conservation practices help to maintain our national parks, national forests, wilderness areas, and wildlife refuges;
evaluate and debate today's balance between the availability of resources and the growth and distribution of human population;
define sustainability in the contexts of agriculture, development, industrial production, and ecosystems;
discuss the prospects for an elevated societal awareness of sound environmental conservation practices from the vantage point of major national and international initiatives.

rows.title: Introduction to Data Science
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze mathematical problems critically using logical methodology,
Communicate mathematical ideas, understand definitions, and interpret concepts
Increase confidence in understanding mathematical concepts, communicating ideas and thinking analytically
objectives: formulate and develop statistical analysis plans to address real-world problems using datasets from economics, business, the social sciences, the natural sciences, document collections, or geographical information;

compose and revise research questions that can be answered with the available data, ensuring that the questions are clearly stated and aligned with the scope of quantitative methods taught in the course. Additionally, the questions are written so that another person can determine what data to collect, how to collect it, and how to determine whether the question has been answered;
integrate theoretical statistical concepts with practical computational skills to perform analyses that produce valid, reproducible, and interpretable results;
distinguish, appraise, and critique different scales of measurement and how measurement choices influence statistical reasoning;
design and select sampling strategies appropriate to a given research context, defend these choices, and evaluate their impact on the credibility and generalizability of results;

connect, compare, and conclude distinctions among sampling techniques including census-taking, intended populations, and accessible populations—defined as the portion of the intended population that can actually be reached or measured under real-world constraints;

appraise how differences between the intended and accessible populations affect the generalizability of results; evaluate the practical limitations of obtaining truly random samples in applied settings; and critique the potential consequences—both intended and unintended—of communicating those results to the public;

assess the methodological differences between observational studies and experiments, create appropriate conclusions for the type of study, including the presence and impact of confounding variables and defend conclusions about causality;
design and generate effective data visualizations with clear titles, axes, scales, and legends using computer scripts, and evaluate their clarity, accuracy, and ability to convey intended messages;
interpret data displays created by others, and explain how the information conveyed can be used to address specific research questions or evaluate quantitative claims;
distinguish and conclude the differences between population distributions and sampling distributions;

apply the Central Limit Theorem to appropriate contexts, and explain when it applies and how it functions as a probability model for the behavior of sample means (or proportions) across repeated sampling;
develop simulations and randomization algorithms to calculate and interpret probabilities integrating probability theory with empirical methods;
compute, interpret, and evaluate measures of central tendency and variability using a programming language, and recommend the most appropriate measures for a given context;
construct, interpret, and evaluate confidence intervals, defend their meaning in context, and recommend conclusions supported by these intervals;
apply the hypothesis testing framework to develop and defend evidence-based conclusions, evaluate the risks of Type I and II errors, and critique the appropriateness of statistical tests;
compile and interpret both theoretical and empirical sampling distributions for p-value calculations, appraising the strength of evidence in the context of the research question;
generate, interpret, and evaluate linear regression models for estimation and prediction avoiding extrapolation;
design and appraise models for comparing two random samples, conclude whether similarities or differences are meaningful, and defend the validity of these conclusions;
integrate machine learning techniques such as clustering and regression to predict outcomes, and critique the reliability and ethical implications of these predictions;
select, define, and organize appropriate data types and variables using programming constructs to develop reproducible and accurate analyses;
compose and implement algorithms using functions, iteration and alternation structures in ways that are clear and contextually appropriate;
devise and apply systematic debugging strategies to evaluate and improve the accuracy of code, and defend corrections with evidence;
compile and manipulate tables programmatically to produce accurate and organized quantitative outputs for use in analysis and presentation;
appraise and critique the social, ethical, and privacy implications of data collection, maintenance, and sharing, defending positions on the responsible use of data;
conclude how ethical considerations influence the credibility of quantitative arguments and recommend practices that support ethical statistical reasoning.

rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Synthesize clinical judgment and nursing knowledge to manage care for critically ill or high-acuity patients.
Application of appropriate nursing interventions to assist the adult client in adaptation to stressors of acute and chronic illnesses.
Collaborate with the client, family, and staff in developing a teaching plan for client's identified knowledge deficits.
Plan and prioritize care for multiple patients in the acute setting.
Successfully demonstrate a variety of nursing skills in the clinical setting.
objectives: Theoretical:
identify and describe scientific principles that form the basis for assessments and nursing interventions which assist clients in adaptation to:
musculoskeletal dysfunction;
acute and chronic neurological dysfunction;
cardiovascular system dysfunction;
acute respiratory failure;
hematological disorders;
pancreatic and biliary dysfunction;
genitourinary disorders;
shock syndromes;
trauma to integument (burns);
disaster and triage management;
organ transplanttion;
Clinical:

application of the integrated theoretical framework that combines the Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM) and the Nursing Process in the formulation of nursing care plans for clients with nursing diagnoses of:
alteration in tissue perfusion;
gas exchange, impaired;
impaired physical mobility;
sensory-perceptual alteration;
urinary elimination, altered patterns;
activity intolerance;
sexual dysfunction;
decreased cardiac output;
fluid volume deficit/excess;
post-trauma syndrome;
collaborate with the client, family, and staff in developing a teaching plan for client's identified knowledge deficits;
discuss specific nutritional recommendations for the client who has disorders of the hepatobiliary system;
discuss specific nutritional recommendations for the client who has disorders of the renal system;
successfully demonstrate the following nursing skills:
nursing assessments: cardiovascular, neurological;
administration of oxygen;
tracheostomy care and suctioning;
chest tubes: assisting with insertion and removal, care of tubes and related assessments;
administration of blood components;
administration of intravenous medications by central and implanted venous access devices;
assistance with diagnostic tests utilized for clients with disorders outlined in theoretical outcomes;
plan and prioritize care for multiple patients in the acute setting;
care for the geriatric client identifying normal changes with aging.

rows.title: Social and Political Philosophy
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon the completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Employ the methods of philosophical inquiry, especially the principles of logic and critical thinking.
Convey understanding of theories of justice, fairness, rights, and human nature.

Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and ideas, including democracy, social contract theory, authoritarianism, liberalism, conservatism, capitalism, socialism, and anarchism.

Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by: Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes, and at least two of the following: Locke, Rousseau, and Rawls.
objectives: Employ the methods of philosophical inquiry, especially the principles of logic and critical thinking to reason clearly, consistently, and carefully about ethics;

Convey understanding of theories of justice, ethics, and human nature according to Plato and Aristotle;

Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and ideas, including democracy and social contract theory;
Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and ideas, including liberalism, conservatism, capitalism, and socialism;
Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories including authoritarianism, libertarianism, anarchism, neo-Marxism, and postmodernism. (Optional)

Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and apply them to at least two of the following contemporary issues: race and affirmative action; terrorism, torture, and surveillance; welfare, poverty, hunger, and wealth inequality; prostitution and pornography; free speech, hate speech, and censorship; technology, artificial intelligence, and piracy; offensive humor, trigger warnings, and cancel culture;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by Plato or Aristotle;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by Hobbes;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by at least two of the following: Locke, Rousseau, and Rawls;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by Confucius, Lao Tzu, Augustine, Machiavelli, Marx, and Arendt. (Optional)

Given sets of premises in Spanish, construct deductive arguments with clear conclusions, including analysis of real-world situations to identify patterns and formulate inductive generalizations;

formulate productive research questions in Spanish based on critically evaluating Spanish persuasive articles, identifying the implicit assumptions underlying the authors’ arguments and analyzing how these assumptions influence the conclusions drawn;
